name: Rejection therapy

card.summary: A self-improvement game of seeking one rejection a day to reduce fear of rejection and build social confidence, which supports approachability and presence.
card.note: Little formal research on the game itself.

quick.overview:
Rejection therapy is a social game created by Jason Comely in which the only goal is to be rejected at least once a day. The aim is to lower fear of rejection through repeated small exposures.

The appearance link is confidence and presence: people who are less anxious about asking and being turned down tend, proponents say, to carry themselves more openly, which they see as part of looking attractive.
quick.how: Players make a request that is likely to be declined, often a small one at first, and count a denial as success. A 30-day version is common and was popularised on TikTok; suggestion cards exist for ideas.[1] Jia Jiang's '100 Days of Rejection Therapy' brought wider attention.[1]
quick.risks: The game is low-risk, though the rules call for considerate behaviour toward the other person.[1] It is not a clinical therapy; Wikipedia says its resemblance to exposure therapy is disputed and notes little formal research.

lead: Rejection therapy is a social self-help game whose single rule is to be rejected at least once per day. It was created by Jason Comely, and Jia Jiang, who found it in 2012, acquired the game in 2016 and still owns it.[1][3]

Its rationale is controlled, repeated exposure to rejection so that players become more resilient, with the idea that less fear of asking and being turned down shows up as more confident, approachable behaviour. Wikipedia describes a resemblance to exposure therapy, with gamification added, but flags that link as disputed, and notes little formal research.[1]

The game gained traction through Jiang's video blog and viral Krispy Kreme request, his TED talks and 2015 book Rejection Proof, and later on TikTok, where the hashtag has drawn nearly four million views.[1][3][2]

chain: Less fear of asking or being turned down
angle.text: Players use it to build the confidence to approach people and speak up, which proponents see as improving how they come across.

infobox: Be rejected at least once a day [1]

paras: The one official rule is being rejected at least once daily; a rejection counts if a request is denied or if the player is outside their comfort zone. The player should be in the vulnerable position and stay sensitive to the other person's feelings, and beginners are advised to start with small rejections.[1] Common coping strategies include mindfulness and a 'three second rule'.[1]

The Rejection Therapy site describes a 30-day challenge in which players draw from suggestion cards, and attributes the card game to Jason Comely.[2] The same site offers a digital course led by Jia Jiang with 27 videos and more than 30 hands-on challenges designed for 30 days, workshops for teams and a rejection resilience assessment.[2]
Wikipedia credits Jason Comely with creating the game; no biographical details or creation date are given there or on the game's website.[1][2]

Jia Jiang was born in Beijing, studied computer science at Brigham Young University and earned an MBA at Duke University in 2009, then worked at Dell and built a social to-do app called Hooplus.[3] According to Wikipedia, he found the game in 2012 after an investor withdrew from the app project about four months in, set himself 100 rejection challenges and documented them as the blog and video series 100 Days of Rejection Therapy, which spread on social media.[1][3] He gave a TEDx talk at TEDxAustin in 2013 and a second at TEDxMtHood in May 2015 that was later featured on TED.com, published the book Rejection Proof on 14 April 2015, acquired the Rejection Therapy site in 2016 and runs the training company Wuju Learning.[1][3] The game's website says his TED talk has passed 10 million views.[2]

Proponents say that repeated, deliberately sought rejections lower the sting of being turned down, make asking for things routine and build confidence in approaching people, which they link to a more open, attractive presence. Jiang's materials frame the practice as overcoming fear of rejection through real-world challenges and sell it for personal growth and for sales teams.[2] The site makes a return-on-investment claim for its team programme without citing a source.[2]
Jiang's viral request to a doughnut shop for Olympic-ring-shaped doughnuts is the best-known example of the approach and is described in Wikipedia as having gone viral.[1]

A TikTok community takes on intentional rejection, popularising a month-long format, and the #rejectiontherapy hashtag has drawn almost four million views according to Wikipedia.[1] The Rejection Therapy site says Jiang has been featured in Business Insider, Inc., Huffington Post, Forbes and Bloomberg Businessweek and that the movement has reached more than 128 million views across platforms.[2]

Wikipedia says the game shares components with exposure therapy, which is a clinical treatment for anxiety, and tags the claim as disputed.[1] A recent randomized trial secondary analysis of exposure therapy in 77 adults with social anxiety or panic disorder examined how positive and negative affect influenced learning during exposure, a clinical setting distinct from the game.[4] A 2026 narrative review of appearance anxiety identifies cognitive behavioural therapy as the most studied intervention and lists peer rejection sensitivity among interpersonal factors.[5] No study has tested the rejection therapy game itself.
No studies found. Clinical research on exposure therapy for social anxiety exists, but it concerns a clinical treatment rather than this game.[4]

timeline.event: Jia Jiang earns an MBA at Duke University.[3]
After his app project loses its investor, Jiang finds the game and starts the 100 Days of Rejection Therapy blog and video series.[1][3]
Jiang gives a TEDx talk at TEDxAustin.[3]
Rejection Proof is published on 14 April; Jiang gives a TEDxMtHood talk in May.[1][3]
Jiang receives Toastmasters International's Golden Gavel Award.[3]

lore.intro: In self-improvement circles, rejection therapy is discussed as a way to reduce approach anxiety and build social confidence, which proponents connect to how attractive and at ease someone comes across.[1][2]

claims.claim: Seeking one rejection a day makes you less afraid of rejection
claims.believers: Players and Jiang describe repeated small rejections as shrinking the fear of asking, and treat each denial as a win.[1][2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says the comparison to exposure therapy is disputed and that there is little formal research on the game.[1]

claims.claim: Confidence from the game makes people look and come across as more attractive
claims.believers: Proponents say people who are comfortable being turned down carry themselves more openly.[2]
claims.experts: No published study has tested the game's effect on perceived attractiveness.

claims.claim: Starting small makes the challenge workable
claims.believers: The rules advise beginners to start with small rejections.[1]
claims.experts: Exposure therapy research, a separate clinical practice, studies gradual exposure in anxiety treatment.[4]
